consumedBy.rubricGoesTo: the grading authority, not the assessment engine. packages/assessment cannot hold a rubric by design, so `entries[].rubric` is addressed to packages/grading and is kept in this file only so the item and its line are read together.

gradingPolicy.inheritsWhat: The whole of it — the binary verdict space, the decision procedure, the ignore list, the never-sufficient list, the untrusted-input rule, and the calibration read off the twelve TEA-scored responses in content/staar/eval. Nothing in that policy is relaxed here and none of it is restated; a grader should be given that policy and then these three amendments.
gradingPolicy.whyThisSurfaceIsStricter: A duel round is worth the difference between fourteen balls and seven. This is worth the concept. Mastery is all-or-nothing across the two items on a form, so a single false negative denies the concept, and denying the concept denies the chapter unlock and every PvP-legal Codex card hanging off it.

theseItemsAreAlsoPvPContent.what: The nine prose items in this file are shared into the PvP duel pool. content/m1/duel-items.json -> pvpPool composes them with the PvE duel items and the PvP-only items, and carries the current totals. They were not rewritten for it: same rubric, same policy, same binary.
theseItemsAreAlsoPvPContent.rule: PvP may draw a capstone item only for a concept this profile has already mastered.
theseItemsAreAlsoPvPContent.whyThisFileCaresAboutIt: Without the guard, a duel could serve a gate item before the gate is sat, and the capstone's first-attempt score — the number a teacher is told — would be measuring recall of a duel. The full statement, the pseudocode and the reasoning live with the pool in duel-items.json; the rule is repeated here word for word because a reader of these items must not have to go looking for the condition on their reuse. verify.mjs asserts the two copies are identical.

amendments.rule: Every accept list here is deliberately wider than its duel equivalent, and where a duel rubric and a capstone rubric disagree about the same wording, the capstone's reading wins on the capstone.

There is no grant-on-timeout on this surface. packages/assessment has no GRADING_TIMEOUT verdict source, because a timeout here would hand out mastery, a chapter unlock and a permanent PvP card for a response nobody graded; the attempt stays open instead.

Every item carries `falseNegativeRisk`. On a HIGH item, a WRONG verdict should reach the review log even when the classifier is confident, because that is the verdict most likely to be the one a human review of attempt 1 later revises.

gradingPolicy.whatIsNotRelaxed: A restatement of the prompt, a bare choice on a two-way question the prompt asked a reason for, generic affect, and naming without explaining are wrong here exactly as they are in the duel. Widening the accept list is not the same as lowering the bar.

descriptor.prompt: Set out, in order, how a crowd's action in the harbour became a whole town's punishment. Start from what the crowd did and end at who the closure falls on. Two or three steps is enough.

rubric.requiredCore: A chain running from the crowd destroying the tea, to Parliament closing the whole harbour in answer, to the closure falling on the entire town rather than on the guilty.
rubric.line: Two links are required: the tea provoking the closure, and the closure landing on the whole town. The word 'punishment' need not appear. What fails is running the chain backwards, stopping at 'they closed the harbour' with no who-it-falls-on, or naming a different cause for the closure.

acceptExamples.text: crowd dumps tea -> parliament shuts the whole port -> everyone in town is ruined not just them
acceptExamples.why: An arrow chain, both links present.

acceptExamples.text: some men threw the tea over. so britain closed the harbour on all of boston. now the fishmonger starves too
the tea got dumped, they punished the town by closing the port, and that hits people who never touched it
acceptExamples.why: In order, the town-wide reach named.

acceptExamples.text: first the tea party, then the port act as payback, and it lands on the whole town

rejectExamples.text: they closed the harbour because of the tax
rejectExamples.why: The wrong cause; the tax is not why the harbour closed.

rejectExamples.text: the town was punished so they dumped the tea
rejectExamples.why: The chain reversed.

rejectExamples.text: parliament closed the port to keep order in the colonies
rejectExamples.why: Ordinary governance, and no chain to who it falls on.

rejectExamples.text: they threw the tea in the water
rejectExamples.why: One event, no chain and no closure.

rubric.reviewNote: A student who writes the two links as one sentence has still ordered them. Do not read the absence of arrows or numbers as the absence of a chain.

authoring.distinctFrom: The released items ask what the response was. This asks the student to chain the provocation to the punishment and name who the punishment reaches.

descriptor.prompt: A classmate writes that the Port Act was fair, because it only punished the men who threw the tea into the harbour. Correct him, and say who the closure actually fell on.

rubric.requiredCore: The Port Act did not fall only on the tea-dumpers; closing the harbour fell on the whole town, the innocent alongside the guilty.
rubric.line: The correction must move off 'only the guilty' and land on the whole town. A bare 'he's wrong' with no who-it-fell-on fails, and correcting some other thing (the cost, the tax) fails.

acceptExamples.text: no, it shut the whole port. everyone who worked the water lost their living, not just the tea men
acceptExamples.why: The denial and the whole-town reach.

acceptExamples.text: hes wrong. closing the harbour hits the whole town, guilty or not
the men who did it werent the only ones punished. the fishmonger who stayed home is ruined too

rejectExamples.text: hes right, only the guilty paid
rejectExamples.why: Agrees with the error the item exists to catch.

rejectExamples.text: hes wrong because the tea wasnt that expensive
rejectExamples.why: Corrects the cost, not who it fell on.

rejectExamples.text: hes wrong
rejectExamples.why: Bare contradiction. Nothing shows who the closure reached.

authoring.distinctFrom: The selected-response boundary item asks what the Acts were; this asks the student to overturn the stated misconception that the closure was aimed only at the guilty.

descriptor.prompt: Imagine Parliament had instead fined and tried only the men who dumped the tea, and left the harbour open. Would that still have been a punishment of the whole town of Boston? Answer, and explain what makes the real Act different.

rubric.requiredCore: No — fining and trying only the guilty falls on those men alone; the real Act punished the whole town because closing the harbour ruins the innocent, who depend on the port too.
rubric.line: The reason has to be that the real Act reaches the whole town while a fine reaches the guilty. A bare no fails; 'no, because the harbour stayed open so only the guilty are hit' passes. A student who answers the difference without a yes or no is correct if the difference is the reach.

acceptExamples.text: no. that would only hit the guilty. the real act closed the port so it hit everybody
no, a fine is just for the men who did it. shutting the harbour is what makes it the whole towns punishment
that wouldnt punish the town, only the tea party. the difference is the closure ruins people who did nothing
acceptExamples.why: The reach as the difference, without a bare yes or no.

rejectExamples.text: yes, its all a punishment either way
rejectExamples.why: Denies the difference the item is.

rejectExamples.text: no because fines are cheaper than losing the harbour
rejectExamples.why: Cost, not the reach.

rejectExamples.text: yes because the whole town is guilty for letting it happen
rejectExamples.why: Collective guilt, which the concept rejects.

rubric.reviewNote: The hardest of the three to grade: a correct answer can arrive as a bare difference with no yes or no in it. Any WRONG verdict here is worth a human eye.

authoring.distinctFrom: A counterfactual Parliament the module never describes. Nothing else in the pool asks the student to run the collective-punishment test against a case that did not happen.

descriptor.prompt: A student writes that the colonists objected to the Stamp Act because three pence was more than they could afford. Correct that, and say what the objection actually rested on.

rubric.requiredCore: The objection was not the amount; it was that the tax was laid by a body the colonists had not elected — taxation without their consent.
rubric.line: The answer must move the ground off cost and name where it lands. Any wording of consent or of who laid it counts, including 'we had no say'. A denial with nothing named fails, and so does a correction that lands on some other grievance.

acceptExamples.text: it wasnt the money, it was that parliament had no right to because we never voted for them
wrong. theyd have said the same about one penny. the problem is who taxed them
acceptExamples.why: Cost dismissed by the counterfactual, ground named.

acceptExamples.text: the objection was being taxed by people they had no say in choosing
acceptExamples.why: Ground named without ever mentioning cost, which is fine — the prompt supplies the cost claim.

acceptExamples.text: not the price. they wanted their own assembly to be the one taxing them

rejectExamples.text: shes right, three pence was a lot back then
rejectExamples.why: Agrees with the error.

rejectExamples.text: shes wrong
rejectExamples.why: Bare contradiction with no ground.

rejectExamples.text: it was because the british were treating them unfairly
rejectExamples.why: Generic affect. TEA's scorers give this shape no credit.

rejectExamples.text: it was because they wanted to be an independent country
rejectExamples.why: Independence is years away, and this is the anachronism the concept most often collects.

rejectExamples.text: it was because the money went to britain instead of staying in boston
rejectExamples.why: An economic objection, plausible and not the consent claim.

authoring.distinctFrom: The selected-response BOUNDARY item asks which body could lawfully tax Boston. This asks the student to reject a stated wrong ground and supply the right one.

descriptor.prompt: Set out the colonists' argument in the order its steps depend on. Start from what Boston did and did not elect, and end at why the stamp duty was unjust. Two or three steps is enough.

rubric.requiredCore: A chain running from Boston having elected no member of Parliament, to the tax therefore being laid without the town's consent, to that being what makes it unjust.
rubric.line: Two links are required: the missing representation, and the tax being laid without consent because of it. The word 'unjust' need not appear — ending at 'so we never agreed to it' is the same claim. What fails is running the chain backwards, asserting injustice with no representation step, or substituting a different grievance.

acceptExamples.text: we elect nobody in parliament -> parliament taxed us -> so we never agreed to it
acceptExamples.why: An arrow chain is a chain, and both links are there.

acceptExamples.text: boston has no members in parliament. so when parliament taxes boston, nobody boston chose voted for it. thats not our consent
no vote, no consent, unjust
first, we only elect our own assembly and nobody in london. second, london taxed us anyway. so the tax was put on us by people we never picked

rejectExamples.text: the tax was unjust, so the colonists should have been given representation
rejectExamples.why: The chain reversed. The injustice is the conclusion, not the premise.

rejectExamples.text: it was unjust because three pence was too much for a sheet of paper
rejectExamples.why: Cost, and no representation step.

rejectExamples.text: they wanted to be free of britain so they said the tax was unjust
rejectExamples.why: Independence as the premise, which is both anachronistic and backwards.

rejectExamples.text: parliament was not allowed to make any law at all for the colonies
rejectExamples.why: The over-claim. Boston's own argument disputed the taxing power, not the whole legislative one.

rubric.reviewNote: A student who writes the two links as one sentence rather than as steps has still ordered them. Do not read the absence of numbering as the absence of a chain.

authoring.distinctFrom: Every other representation item asks for one link. This asks for the connection between them, and a student can hold each link separately and be unable to say which depends on which.

descriptor.prompt: The Massachusetts assembly also lays taxes, and the people of Boston pay them without calling them unjust. Explain why the colonists accepted those taxes and not the stamp duty.

rubric.requiredCore: Because Boston elected the assembly and did not elect Parliament — the objection is to being taxed by a body the town had no part in choosing, not to taxation itself.
rubric.line: The distinction has to rest on who was chosen. Any wording of elected-versus-not-elected counts, including 'ours' versus 'theirs' when the student has made clear that ours means the one we vote for. What fails is any distinction drawn on some other axis — size, distance, what the money was spent on — and any answer that denies the premise by claiming the colonists objected to both.

acceptExamples.text: because we voted for the assembly and we never voted for parliament
the assembly is ours, we chose those men. nobody chose the ones in parliament
its not about paying taxes, its about who decides them. we picked the assembly
acceptExamples.why: Names the axis and then applies it.

acceptExamples.text: a tax from people you elected is one you agreed to. a tax from people you didnt is one done to you
acceptExamples.why: The principle generalised. More than the item asked for.

rejectExamples.text: because the assembly's taxes were smaller
rejectExamples.why: Size. The cost axis again, in its most plausible form.

rejectExamples.text: because the assembly was right there in massachusetts and parliament was far away
rejectExamples.why: Distance. The rebuttal Boston's own case does not make.

rejectExamples.text: because the assembly spent the money on boston and parliament spent it on britain
rejectExamples.why: Where the money goes. Reasonable-sounding and not the consent claim.

rejectExamples.text: they didnt accept either one, they hated all taxes
rejectExamples.why: Denies the premise, and denies the concept with it.

rubric.reviewNote: The item that separates a student who holds the consent principle from one who has learned that taxes were bad, and its correct answers arrive in the widest range of wordings. Every WRONG verdict here should be reviewed before it costs anyone a card.

authoring.distinctFrom: Nothing else in the chapter asks the student to explain a tax the colonists ACCEPTED. The module states the fact in one clause — that Boston's own men could tax the town — and this is the only item that makes the student do something with it.

descriptor.prompt: A classmate writes that the colonists answered the Coercive Acts by declaring war on Britain. Correct him, and say what they actually did.

rubric.requiredCore: The colonists did not declare war in 1774; they answered with non-importation — agreeing to stop buying British goods — together with petition and a congress.
rubric.line: The correction must deny the war and name the real answer (boycott or non-importation, or petition or congress). A bare 'he's wrong' with nothing in its place fails; agreeing fails.

acceptExamples.text: no, they didnt go to war. they stopped buying british goods
hes wrong. they boycotted britain and sent petitions, no war yet
not war. they signed the covenant not to import anything from britain

rejectExamples.text: hes right, they went to war
rejectExamples.why: Agrees with the 28% error.

rejectExamples.text: hes wrong because a war would cost too much
rejectExamples.why: Corrects the wrong thing; names no real answer.

rejectExamples.text: hes wrong
rejectExamples.why: Bare contradiction. Nothing shows what they did do.

authoring.distinctFrom: The selected-response RECALL item names the answer from four options; this asks the student to produce it against the stated war error.

descriptor.prompt: Two men explain why the boycott works. One says it frightens the King into giving in. The other says British merchants lose money and press Parliament. Choose the one the history supports, and give the reason you chose it.

rubric.requiredCore: The second: the boycott works because Britain's own merchants lose the colonial trade and press Parliament to relent.
rubric.line: The choice plus a reason tied to British merchants losing money and pressuring Parliament. Either direction of the reason counts. A bare choice on a two-way question fails and the prompt says a reason is wanted; choosing on 'it scares the king' fails.

acceptExamples.text: the second one. british sellers lose money and lean on parliament
the merchant one. it hurts britains own traders so they complain to parliament
number two, because the pressure comes from britains own people, not from scaring anyone
acceptExamples.why: The mechanism, refuting the other on its own axis.

rejectExamples.text: the first, it scares the king into stopping
rejectExamples.why: The fear mechanism, which the concept rejects.

rejectExamples.text: both are kind of true
rejectExamples.why: Refuses the discrimination the item is.

rejectExamples.text: the second one
rejectExamples.why: A bare choice after the prompt asked for the reason.

rubric.reviewNote: A student who says the King feels it BECAUSE his merchants complain has the mechanism through the King; read for the merchant-pressure link rather than for the word 'Parliament'.

authoring.distinctFrom: The other resistance items ask what the answer was. This arbitrates between two accounts of why it works, only one of which is the taught mechanism.

descriptor.prompt: A Boston merchant has a warehouse of British cloth he already paid for, and he loses money every week the boycott holds. Why might he sign the non-importation pledge anyway? Explain what the pledge is meant to do.

rubric.requiredCore: He signs because the pledge is a collective effort to make Britain's merchants lose the colonial trade and pressure Parliament to repeal the Acts — the shared pressure is worth his short-term loss.
rubric.line: The reason has to connect his signing to the collective pressure on Parliament through British trade. 'To help force parliament to back down by hurting british trade' carries it. 'Because he has to' or 'because he's patriotic' alone is thin — accept it only if the pressure aim is also there.

acceptExamples.text: because if everyone stops buying, britains merchants lose out and parliament caves. thats worth more than his cloth
acceptExamples.why: The collective mechanism and his trade-off.

acceptExamples.text: the pledge only works if they all do it together, so britain feels it and reopens the port
acceptExamples.why: The shared pressure and its aim.

acceptExamples.text: he signs to add to the pressure. one shop means nothing, the whole town not buying is what moves parliament

rejectExamples.text: because he wants to make more money
rejectExamples.why: Inverts his interest; the boycott costs him.

rejectExamples.text: because he hates the british
rejectExamples.why: Affect, no mechanism.

rejectExamples.text: so he doesnt have to pay the tax on it
rejectExamples.why: Confuses the boycott with refusing taxes.

rubric.reviewNote: The hardest resistance item: a correct answer must explain a choice against the merchant's own short-term interest. Watch for answers that name the collective pressure without the word 'Parliament'.

authoring.distinctFrom: Nothing else asks the student to explain why someone would act against their own immediate interest. The concept is the mechanism, and this is the only item that makes a person weigh it.
